en: The *Sudhanakinnarī-avadāna* from Kṣemendra’s *Avadānakalpalatā* (Avadāna 64): Even for those whose minds are as tender as fresh sprouts, [there may arise] fortitude as hard as a thunderbolt.
Even for great, stainless jewels, there is no transfer of coloration.

Whenever the Teacher— the moon of the nectar-essence of bliss— entered his own capital city, he was earnestly entreated by his father, who was deeply compassionate toward all, for a mere sight of him at the Śākya residence.
Then, then, from her palace, the deer-eyed Yaśodharā, having made the beauty of her eyes into an ear-ornament,
beheld that beloved who, by his splendor, was scraping away the wonder of the quarters.
Despairing of union with him or even his embrace, her every hope wandering away, as if fainting from poison,
she cast off her body from the palace, repelling her fortitude as if it were a friend trying to restrain her.
Whenever that virtuous woman, whose limbs were as delicate as young shoots,
cast off her body, at each such moment the Blessed One, his eyes moist with compassion, protected her who was deluded by passion.
Then, on one occasion, when the Blessed One was at the edge of the forest, he was questioned by a group of monks out of curiosity;
he spoke, as if warding off the passion of his lower lip with the moonlight of the radiance of his teeth.
"That Yaśodharā constantly commits such a rash act out of distress during my absence—this robs one of fortitude and bestows delusion; such is the very nature of the distractions caused by passion."
In a previous birth as well, being deluded by Māra, I too experienced, due to separation from her,
a grief that was the cause of intense torment and resulted in the consumption of vast quantities of food.
Formerly, in the excellent city of Hastināpura, which surpassed the city of the gods,
there was a king named Dhana, who was a treasury of the perfection of virtues.
By him the earth was embraced with his arms, Sarasvatī was placed upon his neck,
Lakṣmī was adorned, and fame alone was sent forth as an exile.
To him, by his wife Rāmā, a son was born named Sudhana,
who became renowned for possessing a hundred treasures that appeared spontaneously.
He who always delighted in causing the night-lotus of all branches of knowledge to bloom,
possessed of the arts and of stainless luster, shone like the full moon.
That lord of the earth had a neighboring king named Mahendrasena,
who was honorable and renowned for his great prowess.
Afflicted by that unbearable punishment, which seized all their possessions and was like untimely death itself, the subjects lamented.
In that city, where unrighteousness prevailed and the festivals of virtuous deeds had ceased,
the clouds did not rain as it was scorched by intense affliction.
While that king was hostile, a catastrophe of famine occurred there;
indeed, calamities arise from very calamitous conditions.
Then all the inhabitants of the city, afflicted by their particular sufferings and united in their agitation over the calamity of their wicked ruler, reflected together:
By King Doṣākara, this dull-witted man, the people were utterly closed up by the imposition of fresh taxes,
like a lotus pond by the falling of frost.
This man, ever addicted to evil vices and esteemed by untruthful ministers,
oppresses us to nourish parasites, servants, and singers.
There too, a terrible drought arose through the sinful curse of the king;
it became the mother of famine and a witness to the destruction of the people.
The king is excessively harsh, his attendants are brash, noisy, and foolish,
his ministers are miserly, and the scribes in office— skilled in bitter, deceitful, and crooked ways— are provoked and afflicted with malignant diseases of the mouth.
How can this cruel host, which crushes the wretched, be endured?
"It is heard that there is a glorious king named Dhana, who increases the prosperity of his realm;
let us go to his city, for he is affectionate and will protect us."
The kingdom is like a child to that king who always regards it as such;
in his domain, one lives as if in the house of a father.
Having formed this resolution, they went to Hastināpura, [thinking]:
"Even the body, which is fraught with peril, must be abandoned; how much more so the refuge of a country?"

Having learned that his own city was deserted, King Mahendrasena, filled with intense remorse and indignation, spoke to his great ministers: KAvk_64.25: "Having learned that his own city was deserted, King Mahendrasena, filled with intense remorse and indignation, spoke to his great ministers."
"Residents of my city have set out for the capital of King Dhana," so it was told to us by our secret agents who move in disguise.
If those who were distressed by famine have gone to the city of my enemy,
then in every case there are indeed calamities of the gods occurring in succession.
Or perhaps, out of fear of the king's faults, they have departed in their desire for happiness;
for whose king is there a people released from the burden of forced labor, fines, and taxes?
Generally, because of an aversion to what is familiar and a constant desire for the ever-new,
everyone becomes beloved to everyone else only when they are at a distance.
What quality of that lord of the earth is so superior to ours,
by which he captivates his subjects just as he does his own innocent wife?
"Let a means be devised, then, for the quelling of his pride;
let that which is the cause of his prosperity be thwarted."
Having heard these words of the king, the great ministers spoke:
"Listen, O Lord, to how that king became so preeminent in wealth and people."
In that region there was a Naga king named Citra, who possessed abundant water;
he was like the personified prosperity of that lord of the earth, bound to him by merit.
By its power, the ripening of crops occurs even out of season;
and all the prosperity of kings is rooted in the success of agriculture.
Therefore, if that Naga can be subdued by the power of knowledge,
then his subjects will themselves come to seek refuge in you alone.
Therefore, having sought out some practitioner who possesses the power of a blazing mantra,
let an effort be made quickly to seize the king of the nāgas.
Having heard these words of the minister, the lord of the earth said, "So be it.
For the wicked are devoid of the cultivation of their own virtues and are intent upon proclaiming the faults of others.
Then, having made a proclamation offering a reward of abundant gold,
those ministers found the minister who was an expert in binding the nāgas.
Requested by them through an agreement for the payment of gold, he, known as Vidyādhara,
set out for Hastināpura to bring the painting.
There, at the edge of the forest where the trees were lush and dark green,
he beheld the palace of the lord of serpents, shining like the sky.
A jeweled mirror, serving as a nearby ornament for her whose bakula garlands were swaying and whose tilaka mark was radiant, was like the forest-goddess herself with her nearby decoration.
Beholding that pure water, his mind soiled by longing, he—
equipped with the recitation and meditation of mantras— performed the binding of the directions for the sake of attaining success.
When the binding of the quarters was performed by him of such exceedingly fierce luster,
the lord of serpents, whose crest-jewels were heated, suffered a pain in his head.
Then, rising up invisibly and seeing that practitioner of mantras, the lord of serpents, trembling with fear of his bondage, thought to himself: ||| KAvk_64.44 |||
With tawny eyebrows and beard, variegated with hair as brown as lightning,
resembling Death at an untimely hour, he has come to destroy my lineage.
"In this forest, a blockade has now been established by this evil-minded one;
as long as he does not bind me, a course of stratagem is appropriate."
A great sage named Valkalāyana dwells on the edge of this bank;
I know that he, too, is not capable of effectively protecting me.
In that hermitage, there is a hunter named Padmaka who is always devoted to service; he is capable of protecting me.
Having thus resolved in his mind, he went into the presence of the hunter,
informed him of his own situation, and requested protection from captivity.
Requested by the Naga king for the very purpose of slaying the practitioner,
the archer arrived at that place and beheld the one steadfast in mantra.
At this juncture, the mantra-practitioner, having offered oblations into the fire,
performed the rite of summoning the Naga king, being eager to bind him.

When the lord of serpents was summoned by the mantra, the water of his abode for a moment wept as if with sorrow, its rising bubbles sounding like a sob. (KAvk 64.52) The water, with its bright garlands of foam produced by the force of the sighs of despair from the female serpents who were overwhelmed by terror, and trembling violently with its hands of waves joined in *añjali* as if for protection, seemed to offer a prayer. (KAvk 64.53)
By him, through the power of his knowledge and with the splendor of Garuḍa, the serpent was seized;
its coils were contracted and twisted as it was cast into a water-vessel.
Drawing his bow, the hunter pierced that man, who was greedy for gold and whose eyes were clouded with fear,
with an arrow smeared with poison.
Approaching that man who possessed great arrows but had once again abandoned his snake-weapon,
he severed his head with a formidable sword.
That sorceress, though she had attained her powers, became through greed devoted to another man;
for that deluded one, it resulted solely in his own destruction.
The powers of knowledge and wealth, when employed for the purpose of harming others,
perish instantly along with the lives of those who are utterly deluded.
Then the lord of serpents, filled with great joy, grateful,
and his mind overcome by affection, led that hunter to his own abode.
There, being honored with great splendor in jeweled palaces, pleasure gardens, and celestial mansions adorned with jewel-stems,
he dwelt for some time.
Then, at one time, filled with wonder,
he saw the noose called Amogha, which resembled a streak of lightning, being worshipped by a nāga.
Having seen him and having heard of his power as reported by the Nāga,
the hunter, though greedy-minded, made an earnest effort to obtain him.
The Lord of Serpents affectionately gave him that [weapon], which was invincible even for the gods in the exertion of battle and which bound [its foes], holding it dearer than his own life.
Then, taking that variegated noose and bidding farewell to Citra,
the hunter emerged from the abode of the nāgas and, having achieved his purpose, went to his own home.
Having enjoyed that prosperity for a long time, which he had attained through the power of the nāga,
he passed away after entrusting the noose to his son named Utpalaka.
Observing his father’s conduct,
that young hunter as well became devoted to serving that sage in accordance with the family tradition.

Then once, while the sage was resting, he stood before him and heard a soft, warbling song that was like an elixir for the ears. Beholding the forest—where the deer remained motionless, absorbed in listening to the song—as if it were a scene depicted in a painting, he asked the astonished sage: "This [sound] is like the humming of bees confined within a lotus bud."
"Whence is this sound heard, so charming like the warbling of a cuckoo?"
Thus questioned by the hunter’s son, the sage said to him:
"These kinnara maidens are singing this sweet-sounding song."
Surrounded by a hundred maidens, this Manoharā, the daughter of Druma, the lord of the kinnaras,
sports in the abode of the nāgas with five [companions].
Having heard this, overcome with curiosity, he spoke again to the sage:
"Is it possible for a man to obtain a kinnara maiden?"
The sage said to him: "He who holds in the palm of his hand the noose called Amogha is able to carry off the beloved of the Kinnaras."
Having heard this, the hunter, filled with enthusiasm, bowed to him and then set out toward the vicinity of the lord of serpents' abode,
taking his snare with him.
There he beheld a host of kinnarīs, marked by their playful dalliance,
possessing the beauty of a grove of golden creepers swaying in the breeze.
As they emerged from their bath, he beheld those enchanting women,
like the water-deities who extinguish the fire of the three-eyed god for the sake of Smara.
In youth, which is filled with surging waves of the onset of the amorous play of the bodiless god of love,
she acted as a support for childhood as it was sinking away; she was beautiful with the divine garments fastened by her girdle,
like a broad mass of foam clinging to one engaged in the sport of water-play.
With her large pearl necklace, as if with a vast stream overflowing with loveliness,
she carried away the splendor of the moon-bright night.
Again, she was adjusting with the mass of rays from the gems in her ear-ornaments a playful lotus-stalk that had been moistened by water upon her cheeks.
With a decorative mark on her forehead being drawn by her friend with a streak of musk,
she was dispelling the moon's timidity caused by its possession of a dark spot.
Seeing her, his mind drawn by the noose of overwhelming wonder,
the hunter immediately prepared the noose known as "Infallible."
Then, trembling with terror upon seeing him with noose in hand, those fawn-eyed kinnarīs suddenly flew up into the sky.
With swift hand, he cast his noose and seized Manoharā, whose eyes were wide with terror,
just as a hunter seizes a doe.
Helpless by the noose, dragged by him and fallen into a miserable state,
she did not know what this was, her eyes closed for a moment in a swoon.
Like a doe strayed from the herd, looking toward the quarters of the sky with the hope of seeing her own kin, she, being greatly agitated, addressed him.
"Release me, release me! I am firmly seized; do not touch me, protect me!
For even the cruel become compassionate in times of intense grief."
A divine maiden employed for the sake of the unsurpassed state out of greed immediately burns the practitioner,
like a spell that has been set ablaze.
O wise one, by reflecting upon me with your intellect and bestowing me upon a worthy recipient,
there will certainly come to you a great influx of the wealth of Dharma.
"I cannot endure this suffering caused by your noose; release my bonds!
I shall go of my own accord to wherever you desire to go."
"I leap up into the sky and go, yet I am not one whose bonds are released;
for it is by its power that my movement through the air occurs—take this crest-jewel."
Thus addressed by her, he, moved to compassion and shedding tears,
took his crest-jewel, released the noose, and said to her:
Take heart, O auspicious lady; you ought not to grieve.
I am certainly not bestowing you upon one unworthy of you by my own will.
There was a glorious prince, a great ocean of the jewels of virtue,
by whom all the quarters were filled with the nectar-waves of his fame.
He was a mirror for the learned, adorned with the play of the arts,
of virtuous conduct, named Sudhana, and the ornament of his own lineage.

O fair-browed one, he is worthy of you—a source of playful adornment for the earth, delightful through both renunciation and enjoyment, like a festival of bliss for the Goddess Śrī herself. He is the lord of the night who makes the pride of the celestial, kinnara, gandharva, and vidyādhara beauties seem insignificant. (KAvk 64.96–97)
Thus consoled by him, Manoharā, separated from her circle of kinsmen,
lamented most piteously like a female osprey.
In the meantime, Sudhana, an archer eager for the sport of hunting, set out and slowly arrived at that region on the slopes of the Vindhya mountains.
By the sound of his chariot wheels, the circle of peacocks began to dance,
and for a moment, the forest’s beauty took on the appearance of shimmering blue silk garments.
He shone with drops of perspiration resting upon his cheeks, which,
reflected on the edges of his earrings, resembled lovely pearls fallen from a beautiful woman.
As if removing the mass of dust raised by the hooves of his chariot horses with the luster of his teeth,
he spoke to the charioteer.
Aha! How much ground has been traversed by this chariot, swift as the wind, which seems like a mere wish-fulfiller, having utterly abandoned its own army?
These young *pippala* shoots,
trembling in the gentle breeze and adorned with golden deer, steal away the green luster of the earth.
These flower-clusters, with sprout-like shoots for lips and clusters of blossoms for breasts,
yawn as if full of longing, agitated by the wind.
These forest ranges, clad in garments of emerald-green grass, shine forth,
stained with the pollen of flowers.
These does, fleeing in terror with their necks arched,
create the illusion of groves of blue lotuses with their darting glances.
These young elephants, whose tusks are as lovely as the sprouts of the moon’s rays and whose frontal globes resemble the breasts of the chieftain’s beloveds,
gaze all around my chariot with their ears stilled by the removal of agitation caused by the sound of the wheel-rims.
These [trees], fond of the wild festival of honey from the flowers of the creepers spreading along the banks of the pure Narmadā, appear as if reeling like those intoxicated;
they are adorned with the shimmering peacock-feather garlands on the hips of the Śabara women.
The breezes from the Vindhya mountains [are present] in the binding of the arts of playful swinging, jesting, and amorous grace.
Speaking thus and observing the splendor of the forest,
the prince heard in that desolate place the piteous cry of a kinnarī.
Upon hearing this, the ocean of compassion, drawn by curiosity, approached her;
that mirror of virtuous qualities beheld that fawn-eyed woman.
She was entreating the hunter for protection with tearful eyes,
like a forest deity agitated by the fear of a woodsman.
She had come seeking her own lap, which had been drawn away by the hunter,
appearing like the exhausted Fortune of the Moon who, having wandered through the forest, has returned weary.
Beholding her, he was struck with wonder by the excellence of her extraordinary beauty;
he instantly became like one depicted in a painting upon a canvas of longing.
He thought:
"Aha! In this delineation of a face, the Creator's mastery over the transformation of lines reveals his practice in creating beautiful forms."
In the realm of the serpents, such [beauty] is difficult to find; what need is there to speak of it in the world of mortals?
I believe this seal of loveliness has arisen all afresh even in heaven.

By means of youth, which has swallowed up childhood, a new form of graceful movement— charming through the god of love and a companion to the contact of every limb— was adopted by that slender-limbed woman;
it was a prowess devoid of agitation, achieved without the exertion of vast undertakings.
By her, the Lord whose weapon is his playful charm conquers the sovereignty over the worlds.
Approaching her as if to drink her in with eyes filled with wonder and longing, the hunter bowed and said: KAvk_64.118.
"O King, this daughter of the Kinnara king Drumakalpadruma, who is dear to him,
has been carried off by me with a noose."
"This divine maiden has been brought here for your sake; please accept her.
O noble one in virtue, you alone are as fit to be her husband as the earth is for the world."
"This crest-jewel of hers, which grants the power of moving at will, was taken by me;
deprived of it, she cannot travel through the air."
"This jewel must be guarded; once it is given away, there can be no union with her," saying this, the hunter gave him the jewel and that gem-like maiden.
Once she was taken by Prince Mahīrghalakṣmaṇa,
she abandoned the fire of separation from her own country as if it were sprinkled with nectar.
Smara bound her— who was as restless with longing glances as a young doe abandoned by a hunter— with the snare of passion.
Having placed the kinnarī upon the chariot and filled it with jewels for the hunter,
the prince, full of joy, set out for his own city.
Having reached Hastināpura and related his own story to his father,
he was honored with a wedding festival by that king, who was filled with joy and wonder.

He made a kinnara maiden, who was beloved in the inner apartments and who, through her good deeds, had attained a state of being an object of enjoyment as if she were the very personification of the moon’s splendor.
As he aroused in her a longing for the honey of his lips as if with a bee, she,
her lotus-face bent down upon being touched, trembled like a lotus plant.
Even when she was silent, he expressed his longing; even when she trembled, he remained steadfast;
and even when she felt embarrassed, her radiant beauty shone forth—he thus extended his affection for her.
Having gently applied the threat of his teeth to the taste of her lower lip,
he broke the seal of silence upon her whose eyes were like sleepless lotuses.
At the loosening of the waist-knot and the refusal of the husband and wife to join their lotus-hands,
there arose, as if in a dispute, a trembling sound from the two bracelets.
That tree of enjoyment, with passion as its sprout, blossoming with the flowers of his playful smiles,
and marked by the fruit of his beloved’s breasts, became his object of experience.
In the meantime, two Brahmins from the South, Kapila and Puṣkara,
desiring a livelihood, arrived at the assembly hall of King Dhana.
Those two, praiseworthy for their excellence in learning, obtained the office of domestic priest—one for the protector of the earth and the other for the prince. (KAvk 64.134)
As the two of them were constantly quarreling due to a persistent rivalry,
a deep-seated enmity arose from their mutual desire for the same object.
Due to the fault of hatred, Madalekhā, as it were, caused the magical knowledge to become tarnished upon the faces of those two, Mātaṅga and Yogyanirghāta.

Those for whom the lamp-flame of knowledge— which discriminates between things, is a friend to virtue, and is directed toward illuminating the world— renders the darkness of hatred formidable before them,
are themselves struck down by delusion; devoid of discernment, they are rendered hostile to the birth of goodness.
They were consumed by a fire arising from the oozing of sandalwood, moonstones, and lotuses.
In every step, as he was being refuted by Puṣkara during disputes concerning the Śruti and Smṛti, Kapila, burning with anger, thought to himself: KAvk_64.138.
This man of sharp and intense practice, arrogant with fierce pride, always brings me to embarrassment in the assembly whenever he encounters one of duller practice.
For those of base mind, wisdom serves to deceive their conduct, learning serves the fever of pride,
and wealth serves to obstruct the Dharma.
"Arrogant as he is, he insults me by relying on the protection of the prince;
therefore, I shall strike at his very refuge, which is the root of his glory."
Since the prince is about to perish, it is fitting for me to make an effort through some skillful means;
how else could I endure the withering of my honor?
Thus, with a fierce resolve for evil, he rose up out of hatred toward him;
there is no sin in the world that those possessed by envy will not commit.
How can one whose heart is always pained see the true path,
by whom the collyrium of intense indignation has been applied to his eyes?

Passion is a supreme evil, and the evil of pride is even greater than that; yet in this world, there is no evil more unbearable than the evil of greed— this entire multitude of evils is reckoned as being contained within the person addicted to vice.
He too does not touch the balance of one who possesses a sinful portion, for he is born of hatred.
Then, on one occasion, [he encountered] a cruel vassal named Megha, a dweller of a frontier fort (karvaṭa),
who had slain the dispatched army and was his adversary.
Having heard this, the king, out of anger and with the approval of his ministers, resolved upon the fourth expedient and spoke thus to the prince:
"O Prince, go quickly to destroy the enemy by force;
let this sovereignty, attained through due succession, be free from thorns for you."
This arm of yours, adorned with power at the onset of battle,
shall become the tethering post for the elephant of world-conquest.
When the cloud, its rising intensified by the fury of its assault upon the mountain ranges,
has been destroyed, the quarters of the sky are open to your majesty without any obstacle or obstruction.
What is the use of slaying other weak vassals dwelling on the borders?
That very arrogant one alone must be slain; in his destruction, all successes are achieved.
What wonder is there if Hari destroys a multitude of elephants, his own food ordained by fate;
or if he rends a lion with its clawing, mocking laughter?
That valor of his enters the path of human legend.
Thus commanded by his father, he— whose long-cherished festival of crossing [the ocean] was now imminent,
yet who was restless due to the separation from the Kinnarī— became for a moment as agitated as one on a swing.
Having consoled his beloved wife with efforts consisting of accounts of his imminent return,
he approached his mother at his leisure, prostrated before her, and said:
"The proud daughter of the lord of the Kinnaras, who is like Śakra himself, is afflicted by the sorrow of separation; she must be protected by you with a mind of affection for me."
O Mother, this crest-jewel of hers must be protected, for it grants the power to travel at will;
it should be given away in every way only when there is a threat to one's life.
Having said this, and having placed his beloved— the crest-jewel of women— into his mother’s hand,
he departed swiftly from the army, which covered the quarters of the sky.
The thick mass of dust raised by his multitude of horses, appearing at the end of the day,
became the cause of exhaustion and terror for the royal swans.
When her beloved had gone far away, Manoharā, due to the pangs of separation,
took refuge upon a bed of young lotus leaves.
As she, longing for him, was constantly engaged in counting the days, drawing trembling lines upon the ground that traced the path of the numerical marks,
her hand— its bracelets jingling as they fell through exhaustion— [became thin].
The stream of tears quickly took on the rhythmic patter of a broken string of pearls.

There was hatred for the flower-arrowed god, aversion toward pleasure, lack of affection even for her own body, constant devotion to meditation upon her husband, and the incessant chanting of his name as a mantra;
yet, though her bed was the surface of the earth, no injury from the heat of grief befell that fair-limbed woman.
Surely, for those whose minds have their passion stilled and dissolved, liberation is not attained through rigorous vows.
Reclining on a crystal couch, pale as yellow sandalwood,
that slender woman shone like a crescent moon situated in the midst of the moonlight.
Then once, King Kapila, apprehensive due to a vision in a dream, summoned his domestic priest and questioned him in private.
Today I saw in a dream that my city was besieged by enemies and enveloped by my own entrails,
which had been torn from my ruptured belly and dragged out.
"O Mahāmati, tell me the fruit of this dream that requires ripening; consider a remedy that is auspicious in its outcome and appropriate."
Thus questioned by the lord of the earth, the domestic priest,
maintaining a meditation held through both devotion and hypocrisy, reflected for a moment upon his desired objective.
"By good fortune, this means, which I have long contemplated,
has been found by me for the purpose of destroying Puṣkara's refuge and for the slaughter of the prince."
His beloved, the enchanting Kinnarī, was his very life;
in her absence, he would certainly not live, being consumed by grief.
Having reflected thus, the priest, desiring harm [to the king], spoke slowly to the lord of the earth with feigned distress and dejection: KAvk_64.169.
"O Lord, this most terrifying bad dream has been seen by you; its result is clearly unbearable—how can it be called otherwise? (KAvk 64.170)
For those who are established in the vow of devotion to their lord and whose minds are not intent on finding fault,
there is no prohibition for well-wishers against speaking words that may be harsh to the ear.
The clear fruit of this dream is either a fall from the kingdom or from the body;
for one's own welfare, a remedy must be applied here by those free from doubt.
Having bathed in a lotus pond at a sacrificial site filled with the blood of animals,
you were purified by the Brahmins and became a giver of abundant jewels and gold.
"By offering the fat of a kinnarī into the fire, you will attain merit;
for there is a kinnarī in your inner apartments who is not difficult to obtain as a daughter-in-law."
Having heard these cruel words of his, the king— his face contorted by sin and terrified by such a cruel disposition— addressed him.
How could I venture to kill a woman for the sake of preserving my own life?
Moreover, in the absence of the Kinnarī, my son will certainly not live.
When his request had been thus rejected by the king,
the domestic priest spoke to him again out of an obsession with evil.
"O King, although you are wise, you do not understand the condition of human existence:
neither sovereignty nor life itself should be abandoned when they serve as means for achieving the three goals of life."
Just as wealth, one's own kin, friends, wife, and sons, though lost, may return to a man who remains alive;
yet for one whose life has departed with the mere cessation of the breath, all these things, though present at that very moment, are as if non-existent.
O King, for the sake of life, one's own country, beloved ones, and children are abandoned;
for in this world of living beings, there is nothing dearer than life.
Thus, out of a desire for life, the king was gradually deceived by him through various illustrations; the wicked man considered his own action to be justified.
Then, when the sacrificial rite had commenced with all its preparations well-arranged,
and the lotus-pool had been filled with the blood of animals, [the following occurred].
Having been told the news by the king, her own wife, afflicted with grief at her son’s departure and fearing sin, reflected in private: KAvk_64.183.
"Alas! The king is most foolish, for he has been incited by his priest—who is blinded by delusion—to this great sin of ordering the slaughter of his daughter-in-law."
Even when the limit of death has been fixed and cannot be avoided despite all efforts,
fools still desire life by means of taking the lives of others.
If, out of greed for life, even a daughter-in-law is killed by the king like a foolish female deer,
what shall I say to my son?
"O Mother, this Manoharā, my daughter-in-law, must be protected by you out of maternal affection";
having said this, the son Sudhana departed after entrusting his bride to me.
Therefore, having received the crest-jewel from me, let her depart through the sky;
for there shall be a reunion with her husband while she is still alive.
Having reflected thus, she went with tearful eyes to her daughter-in-law; having informed her of the king's conduct, she spoke again with trembling: KAvk_64.189.
"O child, having fastened this crest-jewel upon yourself, go swiftly through the air;
this king is engaged in evil deeds and does not regard righteous conduct."
"Having gone to the sacrificial ground, you must travel by way of the sky;
otherwise, he will suspect that you have been hidden away by me somewhere."
Having heard these words, Manoharā, pained by her husband’s absence,
guarded her exceedingly dear body with great effort in order to be reunited with him.
Having accepted the crest-jewel given by her mother-in-law and fastened it upon her head,
she was summoned by the king, went to the sacrificial ground, and plunged into the sky.
"O King, this is not fitting for you, that even though he is your beloved son, his wife—who is to be slain—should depart from her own place; may it be well with you, for I am leaving.
Moreover, this prince must be protected, as his fortitude will be shattered by separation from me."
Having said "So be it," she departed with the flickering movements of very slender lightning flashes.
When she had gone, the king, apprehensive of an obstacle to the sacrifice, was addressed by the domestic priest:
"O King, do not entertain any doubt."
"By means of mantras, I summoned the Brahmarākṣasa named Krūra;
your sacrifice was accomplished without obstacle, and by him that Kinnarī was slain."
Thus the king believed his false words to be true;
for the simple-minded are made to dance by the crooked, like wooden puppets in play.
Having returned to her father’s house, the charming Manoharā,
overflowing with joy and carrying her beloved in her heart, related her own adventures.
By her father’s command, for the sake of extinguishing the fragrance of contact with mortals,
she performed her daily bath with five hundred golden jars.
The mortal fragrance of the doe-eyed woman, mixed with the oil of fine sandalwood, gradually faded from her washed body; yet her passion did not.
She found no peace amidst the enjoyments of the divine gardens;
for embodied beings whose passion is fixed elsewhere find no delight anywhere else.
Once, exhausted by separation from her beloved, she, traveling through the sky,
went to that ground at the edge of the forest near the abode of the Nāgas.
Approaching the great seer who was staying at that hermitage site, wearing garments of bark,
she spoke while bowing her face in salutation.
"O Blessed One, you who instructed the hunter,
tell me yourself whether this binding of mine was rightly done."
Having heard these words of hers, his face slightly downcast with shame, the sage said to her: "O simple girl, such is your destiny."
Not knowing that he possessed the Amoghapāśa [sutra], I spoke;
having overheard my words, that rogue hunter bound you.
We do not know the crookedness of those with wicked souls and cruel minds;
we are naturally straightforward and vocal in our proclamation of truth.
Having been addressed thus by the sage, the slender woman spoke to him out of affection:
"O Blessed One, may this rashness of speech from a child be forgiven."
But this little that I say before you is merely a transgression of proper conduct, such as is easily found among women.
That even teachers become guests at one's idle chatter is the very inability to endure the contact with the flames of the fire of separation.
Those who are armored for the removal of suffering and compassionate toward the tormented generally become devoted to their duty even in the face of unfavorable circumstances.
"Though I was released from the hunter's snare with my lamentations,
I have been bound by the prince with an enchanting noose of affection."
That fortunate man named Sudhana, distressed by the fire of separation from me,
will reach your presence if he comes along this path.
Therefore, out of compassion, you must speak these words of mine:
"I remain in my father's house, devoid of happiness due to the exhaustion of separation from you."
Whether out of longing, compassion, innate affection, gratitude, or courtesy,
please come here quickly.
The path to the city of the kinnaras is difficult to traverse and is the locus of hundreds of afflictions;
it is truly not the domain of mortals who possess little vigor, strength, or splendor.
At the edge of this penance grove, a great medicinal herb named Sudhā is seen blazing;
having cooked it with clarified butter, you yourself must drink it.
By its power, having crossed over affliction with sentient beings as your companions,
you shall reach my city by a path as white as the laughter of Kailāsa.
"And this ring of mine, marked with my own sign, must be given to him.
Having said this, she gradually described the difficult path to him.
Having instructed her on the means to counteract obstacles through marvelous methods,
she departed after giving her the ring, while her life was sustained by the bond of hope.
Having heard what she said regarding the marvel of traversing the long distance,
the sage took that very ring and reflected upon it alone.
In the meantime, the prince, having conquered King Megha and taken his treasury,
returned, eager for a sight of his beloved.
He entered his own city, which, with the circles of parasols belonging to the vassal kings,

made the sky resemble the ocean whose foam-smile is in full bloom. Then, having approached the inner apartments, he bowed down before his father, who was trembling from the distress caused by hearing the account of the slaughter of his daughter-in-law.
Seeing his father’s inner apartments with all the people downcast and their festivities destroyed by the dart of grief, he suspected some misfortune.
When no one spoke anything unpleasant to him as he was saying, "Does that slender, heart-stealing woman, afflicted by separation, still live? (KAvk 64.226)
Then his mother said: "My son, your beloved lives;
she has gone away having obtained the crest-jewel, but she is in danger of her life."
Upon hearing this, he suddenly fell to the surface of the earth,
scattering his pearl necklace as if it were a stream of tears upon the ground. Having regained consciousness through waters of yellow sandalwood fragrant with sprays of frost,
he slowly lamented, his voice faltering with sobs.
Where is that beauty of the moon in the sky, that river carrying the nectar of churning,
that effortless pavilion of jewels belonging to the flower-bowed god?

As I traveled far away, constrained by the command of my guru, I could not maintain my composure before that fawn-eyed woman whose eyes were choked with tears; thus, this curse of passion has fallen upon me.
"Give me an answer, O fair-browed one; where have you gone, O enchanting one?
By me, deluded by negligence, you, the deer-eyed one, were not protected."
What splendor can there be for the mortal world when separated from you, compared to my own, which is praiseworthy in the assembly of the gods due to the good fortune of union with you?
Speaking thus softly in the gardens that witnessed his union with his beloved, he himself set out to search for his dearest one.
Having deceived his attendants, he went unobserved during the night;
having reached the edge of the forest, he wandered over both level and uneven ground.
Greatly deluded by the demon of intense passion,
he questioned both sentient and insentient beings as if he were mad.
Speak, my friend, young parrot, to that moon-faced one, the very life-breath of your friend; may you forever enjoy the bimba fruit as a mere fragment of the luster of her lips.
O swan, O white-shouldered one, tell me, you who possess the splendor of a playful lotus ornament—
have you seen that face like a lotus, the abode of fragrance, which is a wave of beauty?
It is she upon whose full breasts a cluster of pearls rolls about.
The creeper of her body hair shines like a strand of moss fallen from a swan.
As he lamented, faltering even on level ground due to the persistence of his intense calamity,
the moon slowly traversed the sky, as if out of compassion, revealing the path with its light.
Seeing the lovely orb of the lord of the night, the kinsman of Love, kissing the sky,
he thought from the peak of his celestial chariot that it was the smiling face of the moon-faced lady revealed to him.
Having finally identified it as nothing but the moon— mute, marked by a stain, possessed of blemish, devoid of grace, and lacking the playfulness of a smile—
the son of the king, as he traveled, questioned it.
But have you, O friend, seen in the sky the deer-marked one, whose beauty is your companion and whose eyes are equal to yours—
she who has attained fame in the world through her connection with the likeness of your face?
Why does he say nothing to me when I have come seeking his words on my beloved? By whom has this favor been granted to him, who is so skilled and cooled by the fulfillment of others' purposes?
But have you ever seen anywhere, O peacock, a woman with breasts like rain clouds, radiant with a gentle flash of lightning,
whose mass of braided hair is adorned with variegated garlands— the very friend of your plumage?
O serpent, have you anywhere seen that female serpent whose crest is adorned with excellent jewels?
Behold, the volleys of venom released by her burn me in this unbearable separation.
O deer, have you seen that playful woman, the queen of the god of love?
For it is through the distribution of her lotus-like sidelong glances that I believe the female deer shine so brightly in the deep forest.

Moreover, O tree, have you seen at the edge of the forest a woman— her birthplace of grace, with lips as delicate as young shoots, playful and tremulous, like a creeper adorned with clusters of blossoms?
Surely that royal plantain tree was dragged away by this forest elephant out of a desire for an embrace;
or perhaps she has been hidden by him, who resembles a dense cloud, like a digit of the moon.
Thus, as he raved in his madness within the forest groves,
the night— its moon-like face pale as if from grief— passed away.
Having slowly entered a penance grove situated on the bank near the abode of the Nāgas, he questioned the great seer Valkalāyana.

O best of sages, have you seen some fawn-eyed kinnarī whose single braid of hair was darkened by the smoke of the fire of love— fainting from sighs of grief and anxiety over separation here— and who has thus quelled the pride of the moon’s unrivaled beauty?
Having heard these words of the one separated from his beloved, who had reached the state of madness, the sage understood him and spoke to him.
Take heart and rest; let this anguish be abandoned.
I have seen that auspicious lady, the moonlight of your mind.
Like a doe strayed from the herd, though indifferent even to her own life,
she is sustained by the hope of you, like a female elephant dragged by a snare.
Her lotus-face rests upon her hand on a bed of tender leaves;
her body, exhausted by the heat and with its slender form trembling as the garland slips away,
lies like the steadfastness of hope when one's resolve is shattered by the distress of separation from you.
Her mind finds rest nowhere at all; rather, it comes to rest [only] there.
"I am staying in the palace of my father, Drumā, the lord of the kinnaras;
he has sent this message to you: 'You must come quickly.'"
And he gradually pointed out the path to the inaccessible city of the Kinnaras, even for those possessed of vigor, courage, strength, skillful means, fortitude, and enthusiasm.
And for your sake, she has given this jeweled ring,
by the anointing of whose glossy luster the quarters of the sky turn orange.
Having spoken thus, sprinkling him with the nectar of joy and providing him support through fortitude,
the sage gave him a ring and told him the way.
Following the path taught by him and employing the prescribed means,
the steadfast prince set out to travel toward the direction inhabited by the Giver of Wealth.
Having drunk that perfected nectar-like great medicinal herb prepared with ghee, he—
having attained the majesty of supernatural power and strength— proceeded slowly, equipped with his weapons.
Through his supernatural power, all his requisites were brought near along the road;
for those who assist living beings, all riches are under their own command.
Then, having crossed the Himavat, which possessed the splendor of the playful laughter of the wives of the Vidyādharas,
he reached Mount Kukūla.
Having accepted the monkey leader named Vāyuvega there with offerings of fruit,
he mounted him and crossed over that mountain.
Then,
having slain a terrible serpent as if it were a host of obstacles with his arrow, he passed over the mountain named Ajapatha.
Having subdued the Rākṣasī, who could assume any form at will, with the sounds of his lute, he,
the beloved of the Kinnarīs, crossed over Mount Kāmarūpa and proceeded onward.
Then, exceedingly reckless, the powerful man ascended the single-peaked mountain by means of weapon-pikes driven into it with blows from his mallet.
Then, having ascended even higher to the mountain called Vajraka,
he beheld a flesh-seeking rākṣasī in the form of a vulture.
Covered by a deerskin,
he stood at the foot of that mountain with his body motionless.
A night-stalking female demon in the form of a vulture, greedy for flesh and possessing a terrifying body, lifted him up and placed him on the peak of the mountain to devour him.
Having slain her and cast aside his deer-skin, that valiant hero reached Mount Khādira,
which was densely covered with khadira trees.
Having entered that cave, he found a medicinal herb placed within a stone slab, which dispels the fear of cold, heat, darkness, serpents, rākṣasas, and other such dangers.
Having reached those two mechanical mountains that were destructive to life through their collisions,
he severed the mechanical pegs with the tips of his arrows and rendered them motionless.
Having split open the gate of the machine by means of the complete destruction of the machine's bolts,
he likewise [destroyed] the cutting machine-wheel and the iron parts joined to the machine.
There were two men dealing severe blows, and two unbearable rams;
likewise, there were two crocodile-demons with fierce teeth that crushed [their prey].
And having leaped over a cave-pit deep with terrible darkness, having crossed a lofty river, and having slain the rākṣasas dwelling on its banks; KAvk_64.276.
[He saw] the river named Pataṅgā, its waters filled with venomous serpents,
and the river Rodinī, on whose banks were the servant-maidens of the Kinnaras.
They create obstacles with the sounds of their weeping for those whose minds are fixed upon them;
likewise, they create obstacles for those whose minds are stolen by laughter through a woman named Hāsinī.
Having crossed other rivers, they then reached the river Vetra, upon whose sandy banks the wives of the kinnaras proclaim their own misfortune.
Then, desiring to cross that river, he who was clinging to a cane-stick at the bank reached a vine of reeds on the opposite shore,
which had been driven there by the wind.
Having reached the further shore by means of her, as if by an exceedingly long boat,
he beheld the city of the Kinnaras with its vast palaces of crystal.
Having entered slowly and reached his beloved golden lotus pond,
he climbed a tree on its bank and remained there, enveloped by jeweled creepers.
There he saw kinnara women carrying water in golden jars, which was fragrant and turned yellowish-brown by the masses of lotus pollen.
Having approached one woman there who was distressed by fatigue from lifting a water-jar,
he offered assistance by lending her a hand and questioned her gently.
"O mothers, for whose sake is this water being carried with such effort,
that you do not consider this exertion as a labor performed out of devotion?"
Thus questioned by him with affectionate words,
she spoke to him in an instant, her heart leaning toward his beauty that was the very pinnacle of sweetness.
To dispel the odor of mortals, Manoharā constantly bathes with fragrant waters at the command of her father, the king of the kiṃnaras.
Having heard her say "So be it," he felt as if drenched in nectar for a moment;
he then cast that ring, the token of recognition, into a golden pitcher.
Then, as Manoharā was bathing, a ring fell from her jar onto the pair of her jar-like breasts;
its rays, composed of jewels resembling the sun, quickly attained a beauty comparable to the charm of nail-marks.
Then, as if perceiving her own passion incarnate— a jeweled ring that had entered into the very heart of the discourse on love—
she, realizing her beloved had arrived, asked: "From where did you get this?"
"It has been obtained," she said, as if leaping up, to her maidservant.
Then the maidservant said to her: "O Queen, on the bank of the lotus pond stands a certain lovely youth, like the god of love incarnate."
"This ring was placed by him in this golden jar;
for it causes the water within its luster to take on the beautiful hue of saffron."
Having heard those pleasant words of his, the slender Manoharā,
having ascertained that her beloved had arrived, brought him there by means of that very [device].
Having gone to the lovely garden pavilion where it had been placed by her in great secrecy,
Manoharā beheld it, just as the night-lily beholds the moon.
Through the play of their mutual glances, the communication of the torment of separation,
and the experience of their intense joy, the God of Love attained a beauty encompassing all his limbs.
Whatever was repeatedly practiced within her mind during the time of separation; whatever was taught by Love, that mature friend of joy;
whatever was worthy and appropriate for her affection; and whatever arose from the mass of her longing—[all that she experienced].
The couple performed all those acts, rendered beautiful by their mutual affection.
Then Manoharā, feeling ashamed that her circumstances were hidden,
informed her parents and presented to them her husband, who was like a god of love descended to earth.
Then the king of the kinnaras, his lower lip quivering with anger,
spoke while avoiding the range of vision of the lord of his daughter.
"Alas! Having fallen into negligence through fate upon an unworthy person, O woman of evil conduct, you do not relinquish your passion even though it is being washed away."
Alas! This youthfulness of yours, whose loveliness is envied even by the gods, has through your attachment to mortals come to a state of lamentation.
Born of a noble lineage, full of the abundance of fresh youth,
you have fallen far down, like a river diverted from its course by a violent agitation.
Causing distress to the wise and bringing shame upon your family, you are as loathsome as the foul learning of a rogue; you are not esteemed by anyone.
If you are satisfied with mere physical form, having fallen under the power of mortals,
then why do you not delight in the splendor of a man fashioned of gold?
The beauty of a man who lacks power and virtue, though his form be most lovely, is like the painting of a figure on a wall; it is merely a coloring of a surface.
"O sinful woman, because of the shame of this degraded alliance, my husband is to be slain by me;
I cannot bear to look upon the faces of the gods who have been obtained through your request."
It is true that for a family endowed with energy and distinguished by its prosperity,
a daughter brings about contraction, just as old age does for the body.
Thus rebuked by her father, she spoke to him with downcast face,
while forming a necklace of teardrops upon her breasts.
"O father, it is improper for you to speak thus to me out of anger.
Are men not heard to surpass even the Kinnaras by their own power?"
How could that man be anything other than a ground for [manifesting] supernatural power, who, having crossed this earth— which is difficult even for Garuḍa to traverse— reaches here?
The form of embodied beings truly accords with their virtues;
even the radiance of the moon brings a corresponding joy.
What is accomplished by birth, my dear? Qualities are in accordance with one's own nature.
Is the full moon, which drips with nectar, the brother of the *kālakūṭa* poison?
Some possess inner virtues while others likewise have hidden faults;
one should not attempt to overestimate the value of jewels without having examined them.
Having heard this, the lord of the kinnaras reflected, "So be it," and summoning his son-in-law, spoke to him out of a desire to test his virtues.
These young kiṃnaras have already been surpassed by your beauty;
now that you have displayed your power, it is fitting for you to establish a divine connection.
Having made the vast forest of arrows devoid of arrows in an instant,
and having gathered back every single one that was scattered without exception, give me once more a drona-measure of sesame seeds.
Display your skill in the science of archery, such as hitting a firm target and so forth;
then this captivating banner of fame shall be under your control.
Thus, although the task was impossible, the prince, urged by him out of crookedness,
set about performing everything out of his affection for his beloved.

Perceiving that he was engaged in splitting reeds—a fruit of false ascetic toil—the Thousand-eyed One reflected out of partiality for him: mithyāśramakleśaphale pravṛttaṃ śarapāṭane / taṃ vijñāya sahasrākṣaḥ pakṣapātād acintayat // KAvk_64.318 //
"Is this prince, a Bodhisattva of the Fortunate Aeon,
appointed by the Lord of the Kinnaras to this fruitless labor of affliction and karma?"
Thinking, "I must provide assistance in this task at this time and effort," Śakra brought about the accomplishment of his work.
When the forest of reeds had been uprooted and leveled by yakṣas in the form of boars commanded by Śatakratu, a *droṇa* measure of sesame seeds was sown there.
Having gathered them together into one mass by means of ants created by Śakra,
the prince presented them to the astonished king of the Kinnaras.
That hero, powerful with his strength, having pierced seven golden pillars and seven palm trees—
each joined with a wheel of boars— using a sharp-feathered arrow.
He displayed his prowess with weapons and missiles, as well as his skill in the arts and crafts,
by which divine showers of flowers fell upon his crown.
Although astonished by his power, the king of the kinnaras again devised various stratagems for the sake of deceiving him.
Those of contrary intellect maintain a profound silence regarding vast wonders, laugh during the praise of the virtuous, and turn their faces away with gloom at the excellence of one's fame;
they resort to contentiousness even when propitiated with hundreds of virtues. Indeed, they are utterly intent upon initiating the agitation of mutual humiliation.
He said to him: "This divine power has been manifested by you;
now it is fitting for you to display the excellence of your wisdom."
"Take your own beloved from among these kiṃnarīs, who are indistinguishable in color and form, and who wear identical ornaments and garments."
Having been addressed thus by him, he again beheld before him five hundred kinnarīs, equal in complexion, age, and dress, and remaining unperturbed.
Having discerned her among them all, he took hold of Manoharā,
just as a bee seizes a mango creeper hidden within a thicket of vines.
Having ascertained that he was a god, the lord of the kiṃnaras,
being pleased, then gave him Manoharā along with divine jewels.
Honored with respectful attention by him with praiseworthy wealth and enjoyments,
the prince took leave of him along with his wife and departed for his own city.
Beholding his son arrived at the head of Manoharā,
the king shone like an ocean of nectar produced by the sight of the full moon.
Then, having consecrated his son— who possessed the white parasol of his conduct and who removed the suffering of his subjects— in the kingdom,
the king resorted to the shade of the tree of tranquility, which was delightful with the cool bliss of discernment and contentment.

At dawn, the seven jewels approached Sudhana, who had attained his consecration and possessed vast majesty, as if out of fear of his newly acquired sovereign power, seeking a place to dwell in service to him.
That Bodhisattva was none other than I, Sudhana; and she who was Manoharā was Yaśodharā.
Through the pursuit of sensual desires, I have experienced such intense suffering from the fire of the calamity of separation from her.
Therefore, desire— which dwells within the corners of the eyes of lotus-faced women,

which acts as a hunter in its amorous play with the deer-like wives of tranquility, and by which people are pierced by the deluding arrows of grief and calamity whose tips are like the deadly *hālāhala* poison found in the mass of pollen from blooming flowers— must be avoided by the virtuous.
Thus, having heard that account of his own related by the Jina himself,
the assembly of monks considered the mind-born Lord of Existence (Manobhava) to be full of sap and possessed of a broad root, despite having a hundred branches.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, the *Sudhana-Kinnarī-avadāna*, in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.
